source.title: XRZero-G0: Pushing the Frontier of Dexterous Robotic Manipulation with Interfaces, Quality and Ratios
source.authors: James Wang; Primo Pu; Zephyr Fung; Alex Wang; Sam Wang; Bender Deng; Kevin Wang; Zivid Liu; Chris Pan; Pan-Da Yang; Andy Zhai; Lucy Liang; Shalfun Li; Johnny Sun; Jacky Xu; Will Tian; Kai Yan; Kohler Ye; Scott Li; Qian Wang; Roy Gan; Hao Wang

record.tranche_reason: It tests whether scaling training data improves task performance, using robotic policy success rates rather than held-out language-model loss.
record.gate_note: The study measures robotic task success as robot-free demonstration volume and data mixture vary. These results bear on V6, but it does not measure language-model cross-entropy, fit language-model power laws, test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or measure architectural-shape effects. The reported robotic data-mixing results are not evidence about the language-model claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study is about robot manipulation data collection. It cites Kaplan et al. and uses the phrase 'scaling laws', but it never measures language-model loss and fits no power law. Its only 'scaling' evidence is VLA policy success rates at two demo volumes (300 vs 500 episodes) and three data scales for one task. It measures a different construct (robot policy success versus fine-tuning demonstration count), not any version's system or measure. V5 needs a power-law form, and V6 concerns language-model downstream predictability. So it does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, with additions. The authors also claim the 1:1 mixture raises performance across all tasks, that robot-free data costs about one-twentieth of teleoperation, and that their 2,000-hour dataset enables zero-shot cross-embodiment transfer. They label their results 'scaling laws' but fit no laws and draw no conclusions about language-model scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales robot-manipulation demonstrations and evaluates task success; it does not run language-model pretraining or measure cross-entropy loss.
record.method_sensitivity: Task and robot height vary across the reported scaling evaluations; the text reports 60% success at the unseen H = 0.45m height versus 70% at H = 0.4m for the Flower Arrangement task.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning VLA policies (π0, Wall-OSS) on robot-free demos: success on three grasping tasks rises from 300 to 500 episodes, with Wall-OSS reaching 75% on Eggplant and Banana. On Flower Arrangement, Wall-OSS reaches 70%/60% at 2,000 episodes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robot VLA policy success increases with the volume of robot-free demonstration fine-tuning data (no functional form established).

fits_no_version.finding: Adding 500 robot-free to 500 real-robot episodes raises Inserting Flower success from 50% to 75%. A 10:1 robot-free:real mixture matches a 500-real baseline on Folding Towel (87.5%) and Picking Bananas (75%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A small real-robot anchor plus abundant robot-free data can match real-only datasets of similar total size.

record.problems: The relevant scaling outcomes are described for only a limited range of dataset sizes; the text gives few numerical intermediate points, and reports no uncertainty estimates. It evaluates robotic task success rather than language-model cross-entropy.
record.rows_left_out: Other task-specific values in Figures 6 and 7 are not transcribed because the text does not state them numerically and the flattened figure text does not reliably associate all values with task and condition.

untested.parts: All: no language-model loss is measured.
All: no fitted laws or extrapolation.
All: no architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameters.
No power-law fit in robotics. Only two to three data volumes are reported, without functional-form fitting.
No language-model downstream tasks and no relation to pretraining loss.
All: no exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2/V6 'supports' label should be dropped. The robotic success-rate results are a different system and measure, rest on two to three data points, and have no power-law fit. Figure 6's bottom x-axis is the number of evaluation trials, so the 'robust convergence' is a running-average stabilisation, not a scaling trend. π0.5 results in Figures 6 and 7 are not transcribed. No uncertainty is reported, and the evaluation uses few trials (success rates come in 12.5% steps, suggesting 8 trials).

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger language-model runs from smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation as a function of compute.
Effects of architecture depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes; the study reports task success versus demonstration volume, not power-law loss.
Language-model downstream tasks and relationships between downstream performance and pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices, and departures from single power laws.

rows.subject: π0
rows.operation_detail: Increased pure robot-free demonstration volume from 300 to 500 episodes.

conditions.value: Grasp Grape, Grasp Eggplant, and Grasp Banana

rows.value: positive linear improvement in success rates as data volume increases from 300 to 500 episodes
rows.note: The improvement is stated for the three grasping tasks collectively; separate π0 task rates are not stated in the text.
rows.check: The value is robot policy success at two data volumes (300, 500 episodes). It is not language-model loss or LM downstream performance. Two points cannot show a power law or predictable scaling, and the 'linear' wording is the authors' description of two points.

rows.note: The improvement is stated for the three grasping tasks collectively; the text gives specific 500-episode rates for Eggplant and Banana in R3 and R4.
rows.check: Same as R1: a two-point comparison of robotic success rates, unrelated to any version's system or measure.

rows.subject: Wall-OSS
rows.note: The text states the endpoint rate, but does not give the task's lower-volume rate numerically.
rows.check: This is a single endpoint value (75.0% at 500 episodes) with no lower-volume comparison. It is robotic success, not an LM measure.

rows.subject: Wall-OSS
rows.operation_detail: Scaled pure robot-free data up to 2,000 episodes; the text describes robust convergence as data scales.
rows.note: The text describes robust convergence in the running-average curves but does not give intermediate rates.
rows.check: Two problems with the condition. The Figure 6 bottom panels plot running-average success against number of evaluation trials at fixed data scales (500/1000/2000). So 'convergence' refers to stabilisation over trials, not a trend over data volume. Intermediate data-scale values are not stated, and π0.5 curves are omitted. The measure is not an LM measure.

rows.subject: Wall-OSS
rows.operation_detail: Scaled pure robot-free data up to 2,000 episodes; the text describes robust convergence as data scales.
rows.note: The text describes robust convergence in the running-average curves but does not give intermediate rates.
rows.check: Same as R5: 'convergence' is over evaluation trials, not data scale. It is a single 2,000-episode endpoint (60% at unseen height).

rows.subject: Wall-OSS
rows.operation_detail: Added 500 robot-free episodes to a baseline of 500 real-robot episodes.
rows.note: This is a data-mixture comparison, not a test of language-model loss scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
rows.check: This is a robotic data-mixture comparison and bears on no version.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Pure robot-free data scaling in the three grasping tasks and the Flower Arrangement task
reader_labels.reason: Success rates are reported to improve positively and linearly from 300 to 500 episodes for the grasping tasks, and Wall-OSS is described as converging robustly as the Flower Arrangement dataset scales; see R1, R2, R5, and R6.
